h1: How to become a brewer without a brewing degree
title: Become a Brewer Without a Degree | Craft Beer School
desc: A practical route into brewing without a brewing degree: what employers look for, how to learn, how to get a first job and what to build.
teaser: Many working brewers never studied brewing. Here is a realistic route in, step by step.
standfirst: A brewing degree helps, but it is not the only door. This guide sets out the skills a brewery will test and how to build them from where you are.
sections:
A small brewery needs people who turn up, work clean and learn fast. Brewing is mostly cleaning, moving liquid and recording what happened. Hiring managers value reliability, attention to detail and a calm attitude to repetitive jobs more than a certificate on the wall. A science background helps with the numbers, but it is not required on day one.

Larger breweries and laboratories do ask for formal qualifications in quality or process roles. Look at the jobs you want and read what they ask for, since it differs by company and country.

Ask a brewer what the best new hire did in the first month. The answer is usually dull: they asked before guessing, labelled everything and never left a hose on the floor. Those habits come from care, not from a classroom.

Learn how beer is made from grain to glass: malting, mashing, boiling, fermentation, conditioning and packaging. Learn the four ingredients and what each does. Learn to read a gravity measurement and calculate alcohol: ABV is roughly (OG minus FG) multiplied by 131.25. Start with how to taste beer and beer off-flavours, since a brewer who cannot name a fault cannot fix one.

Books and videos get you started. Structured teaching saves time because someone corrects your mistakes. Our Brewing Fundamentals course is one route. There are others around the world.
Brew at home or on a small system

Employers like candidates who have brewed. Ten batches on a small system teach you more about sanitation, temperature control and patience than any lecture. Keep notes: recipe, mash temperature, original and final gravity, fermentation temperature and your tasting verdict. A notebook of honest results is a fine thing to show at an interview.

Home brewing rules differ by country. In some places it is legal to brew for personal use. In others a licence or permit is needed. Check your national rules.
Get close to a real brewery

Ask to volunteer on a brew day. Offer to help clean tanks, wash kegs or work a bottling shift. Most small breweries are short of hands and glad of reliable help. Be specific: say which days you can come and for how long. Arrive ready for wet floors and early starts.

A taproom job is another entry. You learn the beers, the customers and the business. You get to know the brewers. See starting in a taproom to learn the beer trade.

A short, polite message works best. Say who you are, what you can offer, which days you are free and that you understand brew days are busy. Visit in person if you can. A brewery that says no today may say yes next month when someone leaves.

Brewers repair pumps, read pressure gauges, handle caustic cleaning chemicals safely and lift heavy sacks. Basic mechanical sense, health and safety awareness and a forklift or equivalent certificate (the type differs by country) all make you easier to hire. Spreadsheets matter more each year, since a brewery that tracks yield and loss makes better beer for less money.

Sensory training is a quiet advantage. Judging programmes and tasting courses teach you a shared vocabulary. See becoming a beer judge.

Cleaning chemistry deserves respect. Caustic soda and peracetic acid burn skin and eyes. Learn the protective equipment, the dilution rules and what to do after a splash before you touch a drum.

Write a one-page CV that leads with brewing: courses, home batches, volunteer shifts and a short line on why you want the work. Bring a few bottles or photographs of your batches if invited for a visit. Ask about the job honestly. Expect to start on packaging or cellar work and to earn the brewhouse.

We do not quote salaries here. Pay varies enormously by country, company size and role, so ask during the interview and compare it with local living costs.

1. Months one to three: learn the process and brew your first batches.
  2. Months four to six: volunteer and take a structured course.
  3. Months seven to nine: apply for packaging, cellar or taproom roles.
  4. Months ten to twelve: take on a brewhouse shift and start a quality log.

A degree gives you a broad base. A structured course plus honest practice gives you a working base quickly. If you want one place to start, Brewing Fundamentals gives you the process, the maths and the vocabulary in four weeks of live classes.
faqs: Can I become a head brewer without a degree?
Yes, many have. It usually takes years of practical work, a strong record of consistent beer and some formal training in areas such as quality and safety.
Do I need a science background?
It helps with the maths and chemistry, but breweries teach what they need. Curiosity and care matter more at the start.
It builds good habits. A commercial brewery adds scale, safety and consistency, so combine home experience with time inside a real brewery.
How long does it take to get a first job?
It varies by market and by how much experience you already have. Volunteering often shortens the search.
